description: We are Aeroinformágicos: 3 Aerospace Engineering students from the University of Cádiz (UCA) and 3 Computer Engineering students from the University of Málaga (UMA), all in our 4th year. We are tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge: an intuitive tool to compare lunar landing sites and dates, showing where the Sun and Earth sit above the real terrain horizon. Our mix: orbital mechanics and mission analysis + software, data and web development. Our team is complete!
summary:
When will a Moon landing site see the Sun (power) and the Earth (radio)?

Near the lunar south pole, where NASA plans its crewed Artemis landings, the Sun barely clears the horizon and the Earth stays low. A ridge tens of kilometres away can cut a lander's power or its direct link with Earth for hours or days. Illumination maps give long-term averages, but a mission planner needs dates.

Lunar Sightline is a free web app: https://lunarsightline.pages.dev
Pick a site and a landing date: it shows when the Sun and the Earth are above the real horizon, using NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter terrain data and JPL ephemerides.
• Explore the terrain in 3D, or the real horizon in 2D
• See which ridge blocks the Sun or the Earth, and how far away
• Compare sites side by side, with a verdict and its reason
• Map the south pole and find the spot that keeps both in view the longest
• Check new dates when a launch slips

Validated against independent sources: our Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons within 0.000025°, and we reproduce the solar eclipse the Blue Ghost lander observed on 14 March 2025 within one minute.
details:
The problem

At the lunar south pole the Sun circles the sky only a few degrees above the horizon, and the Earth sits low as well. Whether a lander has power and a direct radio link depends on the terrain around it, sometimes on a mountain tens of kilometres away. NASA's illumination maps say how often a place is lit on average over many years. They do not say whether the Sun and the Earth will be up during your mission, on your dates.

What it does

Lunar Sightline answers that question for any site in its catalogue (the nine candidate landing regions NASA selected in 2024 near the south pole, the other eight regions of its 2022 list, and past landings) or for any latitude and longitude. Blue Ghost 1, IM-1, IM-2, SLIM and Chandrayaan-3 are computed with real terrain; the Luna, Surveyor, Apollo and Chang'e sites use a smooth Moon, clearly labelled. For a landing date and mission length it shows:

- A 3D view of the terrain around the site (LOLA relief near the pole), lit by the Sun at the chosen time, that you can fly over, with a switch to a 2D view of the real horizon with the Sun and the Earth on it;

- A timeline of Sun and Earth elevation, with every sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, Earthset and eclipse;

- The hours of sunlight, of Earth contact and of both together, the longest night, and a verdict in plain English with its reason;

- A terrain profile showing which ridge blocks the Sun or the Earth, and how far away it is;

- A map of the south pole with the share of time each point sees the Sun, the Earth or both;

- A search for the spot that keeps both in view the longest, and a re-planning grid for when a launch slips;

- A simplified power and communications estimate: energy from a reference solar panel, the battery needed for the longest night, and hours of direct link with Earth.

A 60-second guided tour shows a first-time user two real sites 710 m apart: one works and the other does not, and the tour shows why.

How it works

The horizon of each site is computed from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter: 720 directions, one every 0.5 degrees, out to 300 km, taking the Moon's curvature into account, for an observer 2 m above the ground. Near the pole we use the 40 m and 120 m LOLA polar terrain models; elsewhere, SLDEM2015, which combines LOLA with JAXA's Kaguya camera (about 59 m per pixel). The positions of the Sun and the Earth come from NASA JPL's DE440 ephemeris through the SPICE toolkit, in the same lunar reference frame that JPL Horizons uses. The Sun counts as up when the centre of its disc is above the real horizon, and the app also shows how much of the disc is visible.

The south pole map covers 505,344 points on a 500 m grid. Computing their horizons took about 47 minutes on a laptop graphics card (RTX 4060) with PyTorch.

How we validated it

- JPL Horizons: 256 values (azimuth and elevation of the Sun and the Earth at eight sites on eight dates); largest difference 0.000025 degrees.

- Blue Ghost 1 eclipse: the solar eclipse the lander observed on 14 March 2025, reproduced within one minute of the times Firefly Aerospace published (largest difference 47 seconds).

- NASA illumination maps (Mazarico et al. 2011): over the 367,236 cells of the 85 degrees south maps, our Sun and Earth maps correlate with NASA's at r = 0.992 and 0.994, with a mean difference of about 1 percentage point.

These three checks run as automated tests. The app's Validation page lists all 21 checks with their status, including those still pending and one open discrepancy: for the Blue Ghost 1 sunset we predict about 40 minutes later than Firefly's account suggests, probably because of terrain the 59 m map cannot resolve.

Why it matters

Artemis IV, which NASA plans as its first crewed landing near the lunar south pole in 2028, needs sunlight and, for direct radio contact, a clear line to Earth during the surface stay. Choosing a site and a date are linked decisions, and this tool lets a planner, a student or a curious reader see that link in minutes, with the reason behind every number.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SpiceyPy, PyTorch) for the calculations; TypeScript, React, three.js and Vite for the web app; GitHub for the code (https://github.com/aeroinformagicos/lunar-landing-site-navigator); Cloudflare Pages for hosting. Most of the code was written with Claude Code and reviewed and tested by the team (see Use of AI below).

Limitations and next steps

The power and communication figures are a simplified estimate: they do not model dust, temperature, antennas, ground stations or relay satellites. Rise and set times are only as accurate as the terrain map: where the horizon is set by low relief close to the site, a few metres of error in the map shift them by tens of minutes at mid-latitudes and by hours near the poles, where the Sun skims the horizon. Near Shackleton crater, our 500 m map gives a longest night of about 11 days at the best cell, against about 1.5 days published for the best points at finer scale; the Validation page marks this check as manual. Sites outside the loaded terrain fall back to a smooth Moon and are clearly labelled. Next, we would like to add full power and link budgets, terrain slope and permanently shadowed regions, and extend the map to the north pole.

Use of AI

The idea, the physics, the test cases, the reference values and the validation are the team's work. We used AI as a tool:

- Code: Claude Code (Anthropic) wrote most of the source code, tests and deployment scripts from our written specification, one task at a time. After the initial skeleton, every change reached the main branch through a pull request merged by a team member, and the automated tests, including the checks against JPL Horizons and the Blue Ghost 1 eclipse, run on every pull request.

- Text and slides: Claude helped draft the specification, the README and this page, proofread the pitch script and built the slides. The team reviewed all of it.

- Design: the interface started from a mockup made with an AI design tool, and the app's emblem is an SVG written by Claude Code from an AI-generated concept image. The AI-generated concept images kept in the repository (docs/design) carry a visible "AI-generated image" watermark. No NASA logos, flags or mission insignia were used.

- Disclosure: every source file starts with the line "AI-assisted: written with Claude Code, reviewed by team Aeroinformágicos", commits written by the AI carry an "AI-assisted: Claude Code" trailer, the app's footer says it was built with AI assistance, and AI_USAGE.md records, task by task, what the AI generated, what a person reviewed and which reviews are still pending.
